meta.ogDescription: Not Joseph Campbell. The oldest printed credits name the playwright Channing Pollock — decades before the web credited anyone, and still with no source.

answer.label: Not Joseph Campbell — an unsourced saying
answer.authorDates: Originator unidentified · the earliest printed credits name the playwright Channing Pollock (1880–1946); the line also circulates under E. Joseph Cossman and Jackson Pollock
answer.sourceLine: No book, lecture, letter, interview or recording by Joseph Campbell has ever been cited for this sentence, and it does not appear anywhere on Wikiquote’s Joseph Campbell page — not even in its Disputed section. Quote Investigator has no entry for the phrase. The oldest credits anyone has produced are in print, not online: quotation anthologies from 1966 onward set the line as “Love is friendship set to music. —Channing Pollock”, naming the American playwright and critic, decades before Campbell’s name was attached to it. None of those anthologies cites a work of Pollock’s either, so the origin remains unestablished — but it is not Campbell’s.

source.excerpt: Love is a friendship set to music.
trail: Quote Investigator’s own search returns “Nothing Found” ↗ for “friendship set to music” — the standard reference for tracing quotations has never had cause to write this one up.
Wikiquote’s Joseph Campbell page ↗ does not carry the line in any section. The one entry in its Disputed section is a different sentence, about myth being more important and true than history.
Wikiquote’s Love topic page ↗, which collects sourced quotations on the subject alphabetically by author, contains no entry with this wording either.
The online credits contradict each other: PassItOn prints it under Joseph Campbell ↗, Goodreads under E. Joseph Cossman ↗, and QuotePark under Jackson Pollock ↗ — none of them naming a work.

A full-text search of Open Library’s scanned books ↗ finds the credit the web never mentions, and finds it far earlier: Walter A. Heiby’s Live Your Life (Harper & Row, 1966) and Thomas C. Jones’s Words for All Seasons (J. G. Ferguson, 1971) both print “Love is friendship set to music” over the name Channing Pollock, as do Vernon K. McLellan’s Wise Words and Quotes and Clinton T. Howell’s Seasons of Inspiration. Not one of them cites a play, essay or column — so this is an older credit, not a source.
source.excerptNote: There is no fuller passage to show. The sentence has no documented context because it has no documented source — it appears only as a standalone line, first in mid-century quotation anthologies and now on quotation sites, greeting cards and prints.

source.rightsNote: No rights status can be asserted, because no source work has been identified. Copyright attaches to a published work, and nobody has produced the book, lecture, letter or article this sentence first appeared in. The earliest printing anyone has located is a 1966 quotation anthology that merely quotes the line and names no work of its own source — which fixes no origin date and no identifiable author or estate. Treat it as of unknown status rather than assuming it is free to reuse.

author.name: Joseph Campbell
author.heading: Who Joseph Campbell actually was
author.metaLine: 1904–1987 · American scholar of comparative mythology and religion
author.bio: Joseph Campbell was an American writer and a professor of literature at Sarah Lawrence College whose subject was comparative mythology and comparative religion. His best-known books are The Hero with a Thousand Faces (1949) and the four-volume The Masks of God (1959–1968); the interviews he filmed with Bill Moyers were broadcast and published as The Power of Myth in 1988, after his death in October 1987. He is one of the internet’s most reliable magnets for warm, aphoristic lines he never wrote — and this is one of them: nothing in the sourced record of his work contains it.

misattribution.heading: Four names, no source
misattribution.intro: This sentence is unusual not because one famous person is wrongly credited with it, but because four are — and not one of the four credits comes with a work, a date, or a page. The oldest of them is the one the internet has forgotten.

items.why: Inspirational-quote sites print it under his name identified only by occupation — PassItOn gives “Joseph Campbell, lecturer, writer” ↗ and no citation at all. The line is absent from Wikiquote’s Joseph Campbell page ↗, whose Disputed section holds one entirely different sentence, about myth and history.

items.scope: the variant “Love is friendship set to music” (no article)
items.who: Channing Pollock (1880–1946), American playwright and drama critic
items.why: Decades before the line reached the web it was already in print under Pollock’s name. Walter A. Heiby’s Live Your Life (Harper & Row, 1966) sets it as “Love is friendship set to music. —Channing Pollock”; Thomas C. Jones’s Words for All Seasons (J. G. Ferguson, 1971), Vernon K. McLellan’s Wise Words and Quotes and Clinton T. Howell’s Seasons of Inspiration repeat it — all of them findable in Open Library’s full-text index ↗. This is the oldest attestation anybody has produced, and on the documented record Pollock is the strongest candidate. It is still not a source: not one of these anthologies names a play, essay or column of his.

items.scope: the variant “LOVE is a friendship set to music”
items.who: E. Joseph Cossman, American mail-order entrepreneur
items.why: Goodreads files the line under his name ↗ with no book attached. Cossman was Milton Levine’s brother-in-law and mail-order partner — toy soldiers, the spud gun, toy shrunken heads, balloon animals; Wikipedia cites his Los Angeles Times obituary of 19 December 2002 ↗, headlined “E.J. Cossman, 84; Ant Farm, Spud Gun Made Him Fortune”. The Ant Farm itself that article gives to Levine, who founded Uncle Milton’s Toys after spotting an ant mound at a picnic in 1956.

QuotePark credits the abstract expressionist ↗ without citing anything he wrote or said, and the same page also lists a Joseph Campbell version. The print record explains where the painter came from: the old anthologies credit “Channing Pollock”, and several — Mary Jo Heller’s I Thee Wed, Tina Hacker’s For the Bride and Groom — carry the surname alone. Resolve a bare “Pollock” to the most famous Pollock and you get the painter; Nick Beilenson’s Friendship makes the same slip the other way and prints “Edward Pollock”. This is a fourth name, not a fourth claimant.

misattribution.truthLine: The honest answer is that nobody has produced a source — but there is an earliest attestation, and it is not one of the names the web offers. Heiby’s 1966 anthology prints “Love is friendship set to music. —Channing Pollock” ↗, beating every online credit by decades. An anthology entry is a credit, not a citation: no play, essay or column of Pollock’s has ever been pointed to, and Quote Investigator has never worked the phrase up ↗. Origin unestablished — but demonstrably not Campbell’s.

context.heading: Why nobody can produce the source
lead: An aphorism with a real author usually leaves a trail: a page number, a lecture date, a letter, at minimum a book that quotation dictionaries agree on. This one leaves almost nothing — and the little it does leave points away from Joseph Campbell. Every site that prints it under his name identifies him only by occupation — “lecturer, writer” — which is the tell that the compiler had a name and no citation.

The give-away is that the same seven words are simultaneously credited to a mythologist, a mail-order entrepreneur and an abstract expressionist painter, while the oldest printings — quotation anthologies going back to 1966 — credit a fourth man none of those websites mention, the playwright Channing Pollock. They cannot all have coined it, and not one of the credits comes with a work. The 1966 printing is the only fixed point on the whole trail: whatever this sentence is, it was already circulating as Pollock’s a generation before anyone thought to put Campbell’s name on it.
detailsBody: It is also stylistically wrong for Campbell. His writing on love and marriage runs to the difficult and the mythic — marriage as an ordeal, the surrender of the self to a relationship — not to greeting-card compression. The line reads like anonymous sentiment, because as far as the documented record goes, that is what it is.

This does not prove no one said it. It means that as of 24 August 2026 no work has been produced by anybody, and until one is, the honest label is “origin unknown” rather than any of the names attached to it — though Channing Pollock, credited in print in 1966, has by far the strongest claim of the four.
context.pull: Four men are credited with the same seven words. Not one of the four credits names a work.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator has no article investigating "friendship set to music"; a site search returns "Nothing Found".
Wikiquote's Joseph Campbell page does not contain "Love is a friendship set to music" in any section; its Disputed section holds one different entry, about myth and history.
Wikiquote's Love topic page contains no entry with the wording "set to music".
Wikiquote's Friendship topic page contains no entry with the wording "set to music".

Joseph Campbell lived 1904–1987, was an American writer and Sarah Lawrence professor of comparative mythology and religion, and wrote The Hero with a Thousand Faces (1949) and The Masks of God (1959–1968); The Power of Myth appeared in 1988, after his death.
PassItOn prints "Love is a friendship set to music" attributed to "Joseph Campbell lecturer, writer" — that exact descriptor, with no conjunction — and gives no book, date or other citation.
Goodreads attributes "LOVE is a friendship set to music" to E. Joseph Cossman with no source work listed.
QuotePark attributes "Love is friendship set to music" to Jackson Pollock (1912–1956) with no source cited, and the same page also lists a Joseph Campbell version.

Wikipedia cites a Los Angeles Times obituary of 19 December 2002 by Myrna Oliver, "E.J. Cossman, 84; Ant Farm, Spud Gun Made Him Fortune", as the reference for the potato gun. The article's own text names Cossman only as Levine's brother-in-law and partner in toy soldiers, the potato gun, shrunken heads and balloon animals; it credits the Ant Farm to Levine alone, who "was inspired to found Uncle Milton's Toys" after seeing an ant mound at a 1956 picnic. The Ant Farm/Cossman link appears in the obituary headline only.

An Open Library full-text search of scanned books returns multiple printed quotation anthologies attributing "Love is friendship set to music" to Channing Pollock: Walter A. Heiby, Live Your Life ("—Channing Pollock"); Thomas C. Jones, Words for All Seasons; Vernon K. McLellan, Wise Words and Quotes; Clinton T. Howell, Seasons of Inspiration; Charlotte K. LeBaron, Words and Wisdom of Women.

The same full-text index also shows the bare-surname and corrupted forms of that credit: Mary Jo Heller's I Thee Wed and Tina Hacker's For the Bride and Groom print "Pollock" alone, and Nick Beilenson's Friendship prints "Edward Pollock" — the propagation path by which a bare "Pollock" becomes the painter Jackson Pollock.
Open Library catalogue metadata gives Walter A. Heiby's Live Your Life a first publication year of 1966 (Harper & Row) and Thomas C. Jones's Words for All Seasons 1971 (J. G. Ferguson Publishing).
Channing Pollock (1880–1946) was an American playwright, drama critic and screenwriter — a different man from the painter Jackson Pollock (1912–1956).
